newsitem.title: USA: Herd of TB-infected elephants huddle near Chicago.
newsitem.headline: Herd of TB-infected elephants huddle near Chicago.

text.p: A herd of elephants used in circuses that tour the United States was infected with the human strain of tuberculosis, the U.S. Department Agriculture confirmed Monday.
Officials first became aware that the elephants were ill when two of them, Hattie and Joyce who were on tour with the Circus Vargas in California, collapsed and died in August.

"They had lost over 1,000 pounds apiece, and when they did the autopsy they found their lungs were filled with lesions from TB," Mary Beth Sweetland of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) said.
Sweetland said the elephants apparently contracted the strain from humans, but she did not know how or when.

"The problem isn't just for the elephants who are kept in horrendous conditions. Children ride these elephants and health officials have told us that they are more likely than adults to contract TB from the animals," Sweetland said.
There have been no reports of children contracting tuberculosis from the animals, she added.
USDA spokesman Jamie Amberosi said: "It is a big investigation and we're giving it a high priority."
The herd of 18 elephants is owned by Hawthorn Corp., a Richmond, Illinois firm headed by John Cuneo, who did not return repeated phone calls.
Sweetland said the USDA, which has responsibility for monitoring the treatment of exotic animals such as elephants, lions and tigers and enforcing the Animal Welfare Act, failed to act quickly.

Two other elephants from the herd, Lota and Liz, were rented to the Walker Bros. Circus for its tour through Missouri, Minnesota, Tennessee, Alabama and Florida. The tour went from fall until January, Sweetland said.
Florida officials recently obtained a court order barring the infected animals from entering the state, PETA's Sweetland said.

The USDA's Amberosi said inspectors had found that the Hawthorn facility, about an hour's drive northwest of Chicago, met minimum standards for the animals who were now undergoing a special protocol to cure them of the TB.

The Hawthorn Corp has been fined previously for violations of the Animal Welfare Act. It owned Tyke, a 21-year-old African elephant that went on a rampage killing its trainer and injuring another person before it was shot down on the streets of Honolulu in August of 1994.
Hawthorn entered in an agreement with the USDA after the incident and paid a $12,500 fine, Amberosi said.
